title: Chapter 32 — Cetology
paragraphs: Already we are boldly launched upon the deep, but soon we shall be lost in its shoreless, harborless immensities. Before that happens — before the Pequod's weedy hull rolls side by side with the barnacled hulls of the leviathan — it is only sensible, at the outset, to attend to a matter almost indispensable to a thorough and appreciative understanding of the more special leviathanic revelations and allusions of all sorts that are to follow.

What I would now like to put before you is some systematized exhibition of the whale in his broad genera. Yet it is no easy task. Nothing less is attempted here than the classification of the constituents of a chaos. Listen to what the best and latest authorities have laid down.
"No branch of Zoology is so confused as that which is called Cetology," says Captain Scoresby, 1820.

"It is not my intention, were it in my power, to enter into the inquiry as to the true method of dividing the cetacea into groups and families. * * * Utter confusion exists among the historians of this animal" (sperm whale), says Surgeon Beale, A.D. 1839.

"Unfitness to pursue our research in the unfathomable waters." "Impenetrable veil covering our knowledge of the cetacea." "A field strewn with thorns." "All these incomplete indications but serve to torture us naturalists."

Thus speak of the whale the great Cuvier, and John Hunter, and Lesson, those lights of zoology and anatomy. Nevertheless, though there is little real knowledge, there are plenty of books; and so it is, in some small degree, with cetology, the science of whales. Many men, small and great, old and new, landsmen and seamen, have written about the whale, at length or in brief. Run over a few: the Authors of the Bible; Aristotle; Pliny; Aldrovandi; Sir Thomas Browne; Gesner; Ray; Linnaeus; Rondeletius; Willoughby; Green; Artedi; Sibbald; Brisson; Marten; Lacépède; Bonneterre; Desmarest; Baron Cuvier; Frederick Cuvier; John Hunter; Owen; Scoresby; Beale; Bennett; J. Ross Browne; the Author of Miriam Coffin; Olmstead; and the Rev. T. Cheever. But to what ultimate generalizing purpose all these have written, the extracts cited above will show.

Of the names on this list of whale authors, only those after Owen ever saw living whales, and only one of them was a real professional harpooner and whaleman. I mean Captain Scoresby. On the separate subject of the Greenland or right whale, he is the best authority there is. But Scoresby knew nothing and says nothing of the great sperm whale, compared with which the Greenland whale is hardly worth mentioning. And let it be said here that the Greenland whale is a usurper on the throne of the seas. He is not even by any means the largest of the whales. Yet because his claims go back so far, and because of the profound ignorance that, until some seventy years ago, surrounded the then fabulous or utterly unknown sperm whale — an ignorance that to this day still reigns everywhere except in a few scientific retreats and whaling ports — this usurpation has been complete in every way. A look at nearly all the allusions to leviathan in the great poets of past days will satisfy you that the Greenland whale, without a single rival, was to them the monarch of the seas. But the time has at last come for a new proclamation. This is Charing Cross (where London's royal proclamations were read); hear this, good people all — the Greenland whale is deposed — the great sperm whale now reigns!

There are only two books in existence that claim to present the living sperm whale and actually succeed to any degree. Those are Beale's and Bennett's. Both authors were surgeons on English South Sea whale ships, and both are accurate, reliable men. The original material about the sperm whale in their volumes is necessarily small, but what there is of it is excellent in quality, though mostly limited to scientific description. As yet, however, the sperm whale — whether scientific or poetic — lives complete in no literature. Far above all other hunted whales, his is an unwritten life.

Now the various species of whales need some sort of popular, comprehensive classification, if only a rough outline for now, to be filled in later by others. Since no better person steps forward, I offer my own humble efforts. I promise nothing complete, because anything human that claims to be complete must for that very reason be infallibly faulty. I won't attempt detailed anatomical descriptions of the various species — not here, at least — or much description of any kind. My object here is simply to project the draft of a systematization of cetology. I am the architect, not the builder.

But it is a weighty job; no ordinary letter-sorter at the Post Office is up to it. To grope down to the bottom of the sea after them; to have your hands among the unspeakable foundations, ribs, and very pelvis of the world — this is a fearful thing. Who am I to attempt to hook the nose of this leviathan! The terrible taunts in Job might well appall me. Will he (the leviathan) make a covenant with thee? Behold the hope of him is vain! But I have swum through libraries and sailed through oceans; I have dealt with whales with these very hands you can see; I am serious; and I will try. There are some preliminaries to settle.

First: The uncertain, unsettled state of this science of Cetology is shown right in the entrance hall by the fact that in some quarters it is still a moot point whether a whale is a fish. In his System of Nature, 1776, Linnaeus declares, "I hereby separate the whales from the fish." But from my own knowledge, I know that down to the year 1850, sharks and shad, alewives and herring, against Linnaeus's express edict, were still found sharing possession of the same seas with the Leviathan.

The grounds on which Linnaeus would have banished the whales from the waters he states as follows: "On account of their warm two-chambered heart, their lungs, their movable eyelids, their hollow ears, penem intrantem feminam mammis lactantem," and finally, "ex lege naturae jure meritoque" (by the law of nature, justly and deservedly). I submitted all this to my friends Simeon Macey and Charley Coffin, of Nantucket, both messmates of mine on a certain voyage, and they were united in the opinion that the reasons set forth were altogether insufficient. Charley profanely hinted they were humbug.

Let it be known that, setting aside all argument, I take the good old-fashioned position that the whale is a fish, and I call on holy Jonah to back me up. With this fundamental point settled, the next question is: in what internal way does the whale differ from other fish? Linnaeus has given you the details above. But in brief, they are these: lungs and warm blood, whereas all other fish are lungless and cold-blooded.

Next: how shall we define the whale by his obvious external features, so as to label him unmistakably for all time? To be brief, then: a whale is a spouting fish with a horizontal tail. There you have him. However condensed, that definition is the result of expanded meditation. A walrus spouts much like a whale, but the walrus is not a fish because he is amphibious. The last part of the definition is even more decisive when paired with the first. Almost anyone has noticed that all fish familiar to landsmen have not a flat but a vertical — that is, an up-and-down — tail. Whereas among spouting fish, the tail, though it may be similarly shaped, always assumes a horizontal position.

By this definition of what a whale is, I do not in any way shut out of the leviathanic brotherhood any sea creature that the best-informed Nantucketers have so far counted as a whale; nor, on the other hand, do I admit into it any fish that authorities have so far treated as foreign to it.* So all the smaller fish that spout and have horizontal tails must be included in this ground plan of Cetology. Now, then, for the great divisions of the whole host of whales.

*I am aware that, even now, many naturalists count the fish called Lamatins (that is, manatees) and Dugongs (the Pig-fish and Sow-fish of the Coffins of Nantucket) among the whales. But since these pig-fish are a noisy, contemptible lot, mostly skulking in river mouths and feeding on wet hay, and above all since they don't spout, I reject their credentials as whales, and have handed them their passports to leave the Kingdom of Cetology.
First: according to size, I divide the whales into three primary BOOKS (named, like printed books, by size, and subdivided into CHAPTERS), which shall include them all, both small and large.
I. THE FOLIO WHALE; II. THE OCTAVO WHALE; III. THE DUODECIMO WHALE.
As the type of the FOLIO I present the Sperm Whale; of the OCTAVO, the Grampus; of the DUODECIMO, the Porpoise.

FOLIOS. Under this heading I include the following chapters: I. The Sperm Whale; II. The Right Whale; III. The Fin-Back Whale; IV. The Humpbacked Whale; V. The Razor Back Whale; VI. The Sulphur Bottom Whale.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER I (Sperm Whale). — This whale, vaguely known among the English of old as the Trumpa whale, the Physeter whale, and the Anvil Headed whale, is the present Cachalot of the French, the Pottsfich of the Germans, and the Macrocephalus of the Long Words. He is, without doubt, the largest inhabitant of the globe; the most formidable of all whales to encounter; the most majestic in appearance; and lastly, by far the most valuable in commerce, since he is the only creature from which that valuable substance, spermaceti, is obtained. All his peculiarities will be enlarged upon in many other places. It is chiefly his name that concerns me now. Considered philologically, it is absurd. Some centuries ago, when the Sperm whale was almost wholly unknown in his own proper individuality, and when his oil was only accidentally obtained from stranded fish, spermaceti, it would seem, was popularly supposed to come from a creature identical with the one then known in England as the Greenland or Right Whale. It was also thought that this same spermaceti was that quickening humor of the Greenland Whale which the first syllable of the word literally expresses. In those times, too, spermaceti was exceedingly scarce, being used not for light but only as an ointment and medicine. It could only be had from the druggists, the way you buy an ounce of rhubarb nowadays. When, as I suppose, the true nature of spermaceti became known in the course of time, the dealers still kept its original name — no doubt to enhance its value by a notion that so strangely signified its scarcity. And so the name must at last have come to be given to the whale from which this spermaceti was really derived.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER II (Right Whale). — In one respect this is the most venerable of the leviathans, being the first to be regularly hunted by man. It produces the substance commonly known as whalebone or baleen, and the oil known as "whale oil," an inferior product commercially. Among fishermen, he is indiscriminately called by all the following names: The Whale; the Greenland Whale; the Black Whale; the Great Whale; the True Whale; the Right Whale. There is considerable confusion about the identity of the species so multiply baptized. What, then, is the whale I include as the second species of my Folios? It is the Great Mysticetus of the English naturalists, the Greenland Whale of the English whalemen, the Baleine Ordinaire of the French whalemen, and the Growlands Walfish of the Swedes. It is the whale that for more than two centuries has been hunted by the Dutch and English in the Arctic seas, and the whale that American fishermen have long pursued in the Indian Ocean, on the Brazil Banks, on the Northwest Coast, and various other parts of the world designated by them as Right Whale Cruising Grounds.

Some claim to see a difference between the Greenland whale of the English and the right whale of the Americans. But they agree precisely in all their major features, and no one has yet presented a single definitive fact on which to base a real distinction. It is by endless subdivisions based on the most inconclusive differences that some branches of natural history become so repulsively complicated. The right whale will be treated elsewhere at some length, as a way of shedding light on the sperm whale.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER III (Fin-Back). — Under this heading I count a monster which, under the various names of Fin-Back, Tall-Spout, and Long-John, has been seen in almost every sea, and is commonly the whale whose distant jet is so often spotted by passengers crossing the Atlantic on the New York packet routes. In the length he reaches, and in his baleen, the Fin-Back resembles the right whale, but he is less portly in girth and lighter in color, approaching olive. His great lips have a cable-like look, formed by the intertwisting, slanting folds of large wrinkles. His grand distinguishing feature, the fin from which he gets his name, is often a conspicuous object. This fin is some three or four feet long, growing vertically from the rear part of the back, angular in shape, and with a very sharp-pointed end. Even when not the slightest other part of the creature is visible, this isolated fin will at times be seen plainly projecting from the surface. When the sea is moderately calm and lightly marked with spherical ripples, and this gnomon-like fin stands up and casts shadows on the wrinkled surface, it may well be supposed that the watery circle around it somewhat resembles a dial, with its style (the dial's upright pointer) and wavy hour-lines engraved on it. On that Ahaz-dial (the sundial on which, in the Bible, the shadow miraculously went backward) the shadow often goes back. The Fin-Back is not gregarious. He seems a whale-hater, as some men are man-haters. Very shy; always going solitary; rising unexpectedly to the surface in the remotest and most sullen waters; his straight and single lofty jet rising like a tall misanthropic spear on a barren plain; gifted with such wondrous power and speed in swimming as to defy all present pursuit by man — this leviathan seems the banished and unconquerable Cain of his race, bearing as his mark that style upon his back. Because he has baleen in his mouth, the Fin-Back is sometimes grouped with the right whale in a theoretical species called Whalebone whales, that is, whales with baleen. Of these so-called Whalebone whales there would seem to be several varieties, most of which, however, are little known. Broad-nosed whales and beaked whales; pike-headed whales; bunched whales; under-jawed whales and rostrated whales — these are the fishermen's names for a few sorts.

In connection with this name of "Whalebone whales," it is of great importance to mention that, however convenient such a nomenclature may be for referring to some kinds of whales, it is useless to attempt a clear classification of the Leviathan based on either his baleen, or hump, or fin, or teeth — even though those marked parts or features very obviously seem better suited to form the basis of a regular system of Cetology than any other separate bodily distinctions that the whale, in his various kinds, presents. How so? Baleen, hump, back-fin, and teeth: these are things whose peculiarities are scattered indiscriminately among all sorts of whales, without any regard to what their structure may be in other and more essential respects. Thus the sperm whale and the humpbacked whale each has a hump; but there the likeness ends. Then this same humpbacked whale and the Greenland whale each has baleen; but there again the likeness ends. And it is just the same with the other parts mentioned above. In the various sorts of whales, they form such irregular combinations — or, taken one by one, such irregular isolation — as utterly to defy any general system built on such a basis. On this rock every one of the whale-naturalists has split.

But perhaps, you might think, in the whale's internal parts — his anatomy — there we could find the right classification. Not so. What feature of the Greenland whale's anatomy is more striking than his baleen? Yet we have seen that the Greenland whale cannot be correctly classified by his baleen. And if you descend into the bowels of the various leviathans, why, there you will not find distinctions even a fiftieth as useful to the systematizer as the external ones already listed. What remains? Nothing but to take hold of the whales physically, in their full liberal volume, and boldly sort them that way. And this is the bibliographical system I adopt here. It is the only one that can possibly work, for it alone is practical. Let us proceed.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER IV (Humpback). — This whale is often seen off the northern American coast. He has been frequently captured there and towed into harbor. He has a great pack on him like a peddler; or you might call him the Elephant and Castle whale. In any case, his popular name doesn't sufficiently distinguish him, since the sperm whale also has a hump, though a smaller one. His oil is not very valuable. He has baleen. He is the most playful and lighthearted of all the whales, making more joyful foam and white water than any other.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER V (Razor Back). — Of this whale, little is known but his name. I have seen him at a distance off Cape Horn. Of a retiring nature, he eludes both hunters and philosophers. Though no coward, he has never shown any part of himself but his back, which rises in a long, sharp ridge. Let him go. I know little more of him, and neither does anyone else.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER VI (Sulphur Bottom). — Another retiring gentleman, with a brimstone belly, doubtless acquired by scraping along the Tartarian tiles of the underworld in some of his deeper dives. He is seldom seen; at least I have never seen him except in the remoter southern seas, and then always at too great a distance to study his countenance. He is never chased; he would run away with whole rope-walks of line. Marvels are told of him. Farewell, Sulphur Bottom! I can say nothing more that is true of you, and neither can the oldest Nantucketer.
Thus ends BOOK I (Folio), and now begins BOOK II (Octavo).
OCTAVOES.* — These include the whales of middling size, among which may at present be counted: I. the Grampus; II. the Black Fish; III. the Narwhale; IV. the Thrasher; V. the Killer.

*Why this book of whales isn't called the Quarto is quite plain. It's because the whales of this order, though smaller than those of the previous order, still keep a proportional resemblance to them in shape, whereas the bookbinder's Quarto volume, in its dimensions, does not keep the shape of the Folio volume — but the Octavo volume does.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER I (Grampus). — Though this fish, whose loud, sonorous breathing, or rather blowing, has furnished a proverb to landsmen, is so well known a dweller of the deep, he is not popularly classed among whales. But since he possesses all the grand distinctive features of the leviathan, most naturalists have recognized him as one. He is of moderate octavo size, varying from fifteen to twenty-five feet in length, and of corresponding dimensions around the waist. He swims in herds; he is never regularly hunted, though his oil is considerable in quantity, and pretty good for light. Some fishermen regard his approach as a forewarning of the advance of the great sperm whale.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER II (Black Fish). — I give the fishermen's everyday names for all these fish, since as a rule they are the best. Where a name happens to be vague or says little, I'll point that out and suggest another. I do so now with the so-called Black Fish, because blackness is the rule among nearly all whales. So call him the Hyena Whale, if you like. His greed is well known, and since the inner corners of his lips curve upward, he wears a permanent Mephistophelean grin. This whale runs to about sixteen or eighteen feet long on average. He turns up in almost every latitude. He has an odd way of showing his hooked dorsal fin as he swims, which looks rather like a Roman nose. When they have nothing more profitable to do, the sperm whale hunters sometimes catch the Hyena whale to keep up their supply of cheap oil for household use — just as some thrifty housekeepers, when no guests are present and they are entirely on their own, burn smelly tallow instead of sweet-scented wax. Though their blubber is very thin, some of these whales will give you more than thirty gallons of oil.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER III (Narwhale), that is, Nostril whale. — Another instance of a curiously named whale, so named, I suppose, because his peculiar horn was originally mistaken for a peaked nose. The creature is some sixteen feet in length, while its horn averages five feet, though some exceed ten, and even reach fifteen feet. Strictly speaking, this horn is only a lengthened tusk, growing out from the jaw in a line slightly depressed from the horizontal. But it is only found on the sinister side — the left — which has an ill effect, giving its owner something like the look of a clumsy left-handed man. What precise purpose this ivory horn or lance serves, it would be hard to say. It does not seem to be used like the blade of the swordfish and billfish, though some sailors tell me that the Narwhale uses it as a rake for turning over the bottom of the sea for food. Charley Coffin said it was used as an ice-piercer; for the Narwhale, rising to the surface of the Polar Sea and finding it sheeted with ice, thrusts his horn up and so breaks through. But you cannot prove either of these guesses correct. My own opinion is that however the Narwhale may really use this one-sided horn — however that may be — it would certainly be very convenient to him as a paper-folder in reading pamphlets. I have heard the Narwhale called the Tusked whale, the Horned whale, and the Unicorn whale. He is certainly a curious example of the Unicornism to be found in almost every kingdom of animate nature. From certain cloistered old authors I have gathered that this same sea-unicorn's horn was in ancient days regarded as the great antidote against poison, and as such, preparations of it brought immense prices. It was also distilled into volatile salts for fainting ladies, the same way that the horns of the male deer are made into hartshorn. Originally it was in itself considered an object of great curiosity. Black Letter (that is, old books printed in Gothic type) tells me that Sir Martin Frobisher, on his return from that voyage when Queen Bess gallantly waved her jeweled hand to him from a window of Greenwich Palace as his bold ship sailed down the Thames — "when Sir Martin returned from that voyage," says Black Letter, "on bended knees he presented to her highness a prodigious long horn of the Narwhale, which for a long period after hung in the castle at Windsor." An Irish author asserts that the Earl of Leicester, on bended knees, likewise presented to her highness another horn, belonging to a land beast of the unicorn nature.

The Narwhale looks very picturesque, rather like a leopard, with a milk-white base color dotted with round and oblong black spots. His oil is of excellent quality, clear and fine; but he has little of it, and is seldom hunted. He is found mostly in the circumpolar seas.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER IV (Killer). — Of this whale, the Nantucketer knows little with certainty, and the professional naturalist knows nothing at all. From what I have seen of him at a distance, I would say he is about the size of a grampus. He is very savage — a sort of Fiji fish. He sometimes seizes great Folio whales by the lip and hangs there like a leech until the mighty brute is worried to death. The Killer is never hunted. I have never heard what sort of oil he has. His name might be objected to on the grounds of vagueness. For we are all killers, on land and on sea — Bonapartes and sharks included.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER V (Thrasher). — This gentleman is famous for his tail, which he uses like a rod for whipping his enemies. He mounts the Folio whale's back and, as he swims, works his passage by flogging him — as some schoolmasters get through the world by a similar method. Even less is known about the Thrasher than the Killer. Both are outlaws, even in the lawless seas.
Thus ends BOOK II (Octavo), and begins BOOK III (Duodecimo).
DUODECIMOES. — These include the smaller whales: I. The Huzza Porpoise. II. The Algerine Porpoise. III. The Mealy-Mouthed Porpoise.

To those who have not happened to study the subject specially, it may possibly seem strange that fish not commonly exceeding four or five feet should be marshaled among WHALES — a word that, in the popular sense, always conveys an idea of hugeness. But the creatures listed above as Duodecimoes are infallibly whales, by the terms of my definition of what a whale is — that is, a spouting fish with a horizontal tail.

BOOK III (Duodecimo), CHAPTER 1 (Huzza Porpoise). — This is the common porpoise, found almost everywhere on the globe. The name is my own invention, since there is more than one kind of porpoise, and something has to be done to tell them apart. I call him that because he always swims in hilarious schools, which keep flinging themselves skyward on the open sea like caps thrown up in a Fourth-of-July crowd. Sailors usually greet their appearance with delight. Brimming with high spirits, they always come from the breezy waves to windward. They are the lads who always live before the wind. They're thought to be a lucky sign. If you yourself can keep from giving three cheers at the sight of these lively fish, then heaven help you; you haven't got the spirit of godly playfulness in you. A well-fed, plump Huzza Porpoise will give you one good gallon of good oil. But the fine, delicate fluid extracted from his jaws is extremely valuable. Jewelers and watchmakers are eager for it. Sailors put it on their whetstones. Porpoise meat is good eating, you know. It may never have occurred to you that a porpoise spouts. In fact, his spout is so small that it's not easy to make out. But the next time you get the chance, watch him, and you'll see the great Sperm whale himself in miniature.

BOOK III (Duodecimo), CHAPTER II (Algerine Porpoise). — A pirate. Very savage. He is only found, I think, in the Pacific. He is somewhat larger than the Huzza Porpoise but much the same in general build. Provoke him and he'll take on a shark. I've lowered the boats for him many times but have never yet seen him captured.

BOOK III (Duodecimo), CHAPTER III (Mealy-mouthed Porpoise). — The largest kind of Porpoise, and found only in the Pacific, so far as is known. The only English name by which he has so far been called is the fishermen's — Right-Whale Porpoise, from the fact that he is chiefly found near that Folio. In shape he differs somewhat from the Huzza Porpoise, being of a less rotund and jolly girth; indeed, he has quite a neat and gentlemanly figure. He has no fins on his back (most other porpoises have), he has a lovely tail, and sentimental Indian eyes of a hazel hue. But his mealy mouth spoils everything. Though his entire back, down to his side fins, is a deep sable, yet a boundary line called the "bright waist," as distinct as the mark on a ship's hull, streaks him from stem to stern with two separate colors, black above and white below. The white takes in part of his head and the whole of his mouth, which makes him look as if he had just escaped from a felonious visit to a meal-bag. A most mean and mealy aspect! His oil is much like that of the common porpoise.

Beyond the DUODECIMO, this system does not go, since the porpoise is the smallest of the whales. Above, you have all the notable Leviathans. But there is a rabble of uncertain, fleeting, half-mythical whales that I, as an American whaleman, know by reputation but not personally. I will list them by their forecastle names, since such a list may prove valuable to future researchers who may complete what I have only begun. If any of the following whales should be caught and identified, they can easily be added to this system according to their Folio, Octavo, or Duodecimo size: the Bottle-Nose Whale; the Junk Whale; the Pudding-Headed Whale; the Cape Whale; the Leading Whale; the Cannon Whale; the Scragg Whale; the Coppered Whale; the Elephant Whale; the Iceberg Whale; the Quog Whale; the Blue Whale; and so on. From Icelandic, Dutch, and old English sources, other lists of uncertain whales could be quoted, blessed with all manner of outlandish names. But I omit them as completely obsolete, and I can't help suspecting them of being mere sounds, full of Leviathanism, but signifying nothing.

Finally: it was stated at the outset that this system would not be perfected here and now. You can plainly see that I have kept my word. But I now leave my cetological system standing unfinished, even as the great Cathedral of Cologne was left, with the crane still standing atop the uncompleted tower. Small structures may be finished by their first architects. Grand ones, true ones, always leave the capstone to posterity. God keep me from ever completing anything. This whole book is but a draft — no, but the draft of a draft. Oh, Time, Strength, Cash, and Patience!
